title: Hiram of Tyre
lead: Hiram I, king of the Phoenician city of Tyre in the 10th century BC, David's and Solomon's ally, who sent cedar, craftsmen and sailors. A second Hiram, a bronze worker of Tyre, cast the Temple's bronze pillars and furnishings.

sections.b: Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar, carpenters and masons to build David's palace (2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Chronicles 14:1). He supplies cedar and cypress for Solomon's temple in exchange for wheat and oil and makes a treaty with him (1 Kings 5:1–12). Later he receives twenty Galilean towns, which he dislikes and names "Cabul," and sends Solomon gold (1 Kings 9:10–14). His sailors crew Solomon's ships to Ophir (1 Kings 9:26–28; 1 Kings 10:11, 10:22). Chronicles spells his name Huram (2 Chronicles 2:3). The second Hiram, the bronze worker, is the son of a widow of Naphtali and a Tyrian father (1 Kings 7:13–14); Chronicles calls him Huram-abi and says his mother was from Dan (2 Chronicles 2:13–14). Outside the Bible, Josephus quotes the Tyrian historians Menander and Dius for Hiram's reign, his building in Tyre and his contest of riddles with Solomon.
